sections.title: Ulla vs. Rav Nachman: Must the Pedestrian Claim He Lifted It for Himself at the Outset?
sections.gist: The Gemara continues the dispute between Ulla and Rav Nachman over whether *magbiah metziah la'chavero* (lifting a found item on behalf of another) acquires it for the other. Ulla reads the rider Mishnah as a pedestrian who says he meant the item for himself from the start, and the Gemara supports him from the word “at the outset” in the last clause. Rav Nachman reads that word as a contrast, so the pedestrian keeps the item either way.

bullets.text: The setting: Rav Nachman argued that the dispute about *pe'ah* (the corner of the field left for the poor) covers even a poor man gleaning for another poor man. Then the rider Mishnah, which lets the pedestrian keep the item, simply follows the Rabbis, for whom lifting for another doesn't acquire.

Ulla holds that between two poor people all agree the lifting acquires for the other. So he explains the Mishnah as a pedestrian who says he lifted it for himself from the start, and never acted for the rider at all.

The Gemara supports Ulla from the last clause: if he handed it over and only then said “I acquired it at the outset”, he has said nothing. “At the outset” is obvious there, since he can't mean he acquired it after giving it away; it must be written to show that the first clause too speaks of a claim of “at the outset”.

Rav Nachman reads it the other way: the last clause says “at the outset” to set off the first clause, where the pedestrian keeps the item even without such a claim. For him the rider acquires nothing until the item reaches his hands, so even a pedestrian who lifted it for the rider may change his mind.

So the readings divide on whether the pedestrian's intent at the moment of lifting decides. On Ulla's reading, had he lifted it for the rider, the rider would own it from that moment, and the pedestrian could no longer keep it.

Intent can decide this because a *kinyan* is never purely physical: it joins an act to the will to acquire. Even acquiring through one's property without knowing it rests on a presumption that the owner wants the item, and explicit intent can override a presumption.

sections.title: Does Lifting a Found Item for Another Acquire It for Him?
sections.gist: Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda rule that it does not, since it is *tofes le'ba'al chov bi'mkom she'chav la'acherim* (seizing a debtor's goods for one creditor at the other creditors' expense). Rava challenges them from a laborer whose finds go to his employer, which Rav Nachman explains by the laborer's hand being his employer's. R. Chiyya bar Abba, citing R. Yochanan, rules that the lifting does acquire, and reads the Mishnah as a rider who asked only to be handed the item.

chart.title: Rav Nachman vs. Ulla vs. R. Yochanan: does lifting a found item for another acquire it for him?
chart.caption: Each view also explains why the Mishnah's pedestrian may keep the item he lifted at the rider's request.
columns: Why the Mishnah's pedestrian may keep it
rows: Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda
**It does not acquire**: it is like seizing for one creditor at the others' expense
He keeps it even if he lifted it for the rider, who acquires only when it reaches his hands
Ulla
**It acquires**, at least when one poor man gleans *pe'ah* for another
He says he lifted it for himself at the outset
R. Yochanan, reported by R. Chiyya bar Abba
**It acquires**
The rider said “give it to me”, not “acquire it for me”, so he acquires only on receiving it

children.title: Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda: Lifting for Another Is Like Seizing for One Creditor
children.gist: Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda rule that the other person does not acquire. A found item is open equally to everyone, so lifting it for a friend takes that chance away from all the others, just as seizing a debtor's goods for one creditor harms the rest.

bullets.text: Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda: one who lifts a found item on behalf of another does not acquire it for him.

The reason: this is *tofes le'ba'al chov bi'mkom she'chav la'acherim*. A creditor may seize his debtor's goods for himself, but a bystander who seizes them for one creditor, when the debtor owes others too, acquires nothing for him.
A found item is the same: everyone has an equal right to it, and one person can't take that right from all the others for the sake of a friend.

Rashi holds that a formally appointed agent would succeed where a friend doing a favor fails. Tosafot disagrees: an appointment doesn't give anyone the right to take away other people's chance at the item.

Tosafot notes that one could hold that seizing for a creditor fails and still hold that lifting a find for another works, through *migo de'zakhi le'nafshei* (since he could acquire it for himself, he can acquire it for another): the bystander has no claim on the debtor's goods, but the finder could have kept the item. The shiur adds that the other creditors lose a real debt, while other finders lose only a windfall.

children.title: Why a Laborer Hired for “Any Work” Finds for His Employer
children.gist: Rava objects from a baraita: a laborer hired for a set task keeps what he finds, but one hired for “any work” finds for his employer, which looks like lifting for another. Rav Nachman answers with *yad po'el ke'yad ba'al ha'bayit* (a laborer's hand is like his employer's hand), and explains that the laborer's right to quit midday doesn't undo it.

children.title: Rava's Objection: The Laborer's Find Goes to His Employer
children.gist: A baraita lets a laborer keep his find when he was hired to weed or till, but gives it to an employer who said “work for me today”, since finding is work too. Rava takes this as a laborer acquiring for another; Rav Nachman answers that a laborer is different, by *yad po'el ke'yad ba'al ha'bayit*.

bullets.text: Baraita: a laborer's find is his own. That holds when the employer hired him for a set task, “weed for me today” or “till for me today”.
If the employer said “work for me today” without naming a task, the find is the employer's, because finding ownerless items falls within “work”.
Rava: here a laborer acquires a find for someone else, which contradicts Rav Nachman's rule that lifting for another doesn't acquire.
Rav Nachman: a laborer is different, since his hand is like the hand of his employer. While he works, the employer acquires through him.
With a set task, picking up the item isn't the job he was hired for, so it stays his; at most the employer could claim the few minutes of lost work.
This is more than *shelichut* (agency): the binding hire makes the laborer's act of acquiring the employer's own act, so no one else's chance is being taken away on another's behalf.

children.title: A Laborer May Quit Midday: “They Are My Slaves, Not Slaves of Slaves”
children.gist: Rava presses that Rav lets a laborer quit even at midday, which seems to show the laborer never belongs to his employer. Rav Nachman answers that until he quits his hand is the employer's; the right to quit has a separate source, Vayikra 25:55, which forbids a Jew to be bound to another as a slave.

bullets.text: Rava: Rav rules that a laborer may retract and quit even at midday. Doesn't that show the arrangement is built for the laborer's benefit, so that his hand is not his employer's?
Rav Nachman: as long as he hasn't quit, his hand is like the employer's hand. When he quits, he may, but for a different reason.
The reason is the verse “For to Me the children of Israel are slaves” (Vayikra 25:55): they are My slaves, and not slaves of slaves. No Jew may be held to a contract he can't release himself from.
The Gemara holds both ideas together: while the hire lasts, the laborer really is an extension of his employer, but because he can always walk away, that bond never hardens into servitude.

Tosafot: hiring oneself out is permitted as long as the right to quit remains. An *eved Ivri* (Hebrew servant), who can't leave before his term ends, is genuine servitude. The Gra cites Hagahot Maimoni that one may not hire himself out for more than 3 years.

children.title: R. Yochanan: Lifting for Another Acquires, but “Give It to Me” Is Not “Acquire It for Me”
children.gist: R. Chiyya bar Abba reports in R. Yochanan's name that lifting a found item for another does acquire it for him. The Mishnah's rider said only “give it to me”, so he acquires when the item reaches him; had he said “acquire it for me”, he would own it as soon as it was lifted.

bullets.text: R. Chiyya bar Abba in the name of R. Yochanan: one who lifts a found item on behalf of another acquires it for the other, against Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda.

The Mishnah is no difficulty: the rider said “give it to me”, not “acquire it for me”. Asked only to hand it over, the pedestrian lifted it to deliver it, so the rider acquires only when it reaches his possession.
Had the rider said “acquire it for me”, the lifting itself would acquire for him, and the pedestrian could no longer keep it.

That leaves three readings of the Mishnah: lifting for another never acquires (Rav Nachman); it acquires, and the pedestrian kept it by claiming it for himself at the outset (Ulla); or it acquires, but he was asked only to deliver it (R. Yochanan).

returns_to.note: A third way to read the rider Mishnah, alongside Ulla's and Rav Nachman's

sections.title: Mishnah: Falling on a Found Item Doesn't Acquire It
sections.gist: One who falls on a found item to claim it has not acquired it, so another who comes and seizes it keeps it. The seizer performed a recognized act of acquisition, and the one who fell did not.

bullets.text: Mishnah: one saw a found item and fell on it, meaning to acquire it, and another came and seized it. The one who seized it acquired it.
A *kinyan* needs an act of taking possession, such as lifting the item or pulling it toward oneself. Lying on it, however complete the contact, is not such an act.

sections.title: The *Kinyan* of *Arba Amot* and Where It Applies
sections.gist: Reish Lakish, in the name of Abba Kohen Bardela, rules that a person's *arba amot* (the 4 cubits around him) acquire for him everywhere, an enactment so that people won't quarrel over a find. Two Mishnayot seem to contradict him: the poor man who falls on *pe'ah*, and our finder who falls on his find. The Gemara answers that falling shows he chose another mode; Rav Pappa limits the enactment to public land, and Rav Sheshet to places where crowds don't press.

children.title: Reish Lakish: A Person's *Arba Amot* Acquire for Him Everywhere
children.gist: Reish Lakish, in the name of Abba Kohen Bardela, gives the 4 cubits around a person the status of his courtyard for acquiring ownerless items, wherever he stands. The Sages enacted it so that people won't come to quarrel over a find.

bullets.text: Reish Lakish in the name of Abba Kohen Bardela: a person's *arba amot* acquire for him everywhere, as if they were his courtyard.
The reason: it is an enactment of the Sages, so that people won't come to quarrel. If only lifting acquired, two people running for the same item would end up fighting over it.
The *arba amot* work like a portable courtyard: a person's immediate surroundings count as his domain, so the race ends before anyone has to scramble.
Abaye reports that R. Chiyya bar Yosef challenged this from a Mishnah in Pe'ah, and Rava reports that R. Ya'akov bar Idi challenged it from a Mishnah in Nezikin, our own Mishnah.

children.title: The Objection from *Pe'ah*: A Poor Man Who Falls on the Grain
children.gist: A Mishnah in Pe'ah rules that a poor man who throws grain onto the *pe'ah*, falls on it, or spreads his cloak over it acquires nothing, and others may remove him. R. Chiyya bar Yosef asks why his *arba amot* don't acquire it. The Gemara answers that falling shows he didn't want his *arba amot*, and Rav Pappa that the enactment doesn't apply in the owner's field.

bullets.text: Mishnah (Pe'ah 4:3): a poor man took some of the *pe'ah* and threw it on the rest to acquire it; he has nothing of it. If he fell on it or spread his cloak over it, others remove him from it. The same holds for *shikhechah* (a forgotten sheaf left for the poor).
R. Chiyya bar Yosef: if a person's *arba amot* acquire for him everywhere, the grain lying within his 4 cubits should be his.

children.title: Falling on It Shows He Didn't Choose His *Arba Amot*
children.gist: The Gemara first says he never declared that he wished to acquire, but an enactment shouldn't need words. It answers instead that by falling he showed he wanted to acquire by falling and not by his *arba amot*, and falling acquires nothing.

bullets.text: First answer: he didn't say “I will acquire it”, so his acquisition fails.
The Gemara asks: if the Sages enacted that the *arba amot* acquire, what does it matter that he said nothing? The enactment should work without a declaration.

Answer: this case is different. By falling on the grain he revealed that he wants to acquire it by falling, not through the enactment of *arba amot*. Having given up the Sages' mode, and falling being no *kinyan*, he acquires nothing.

The *arba amot* are not an automatic result of nearness; they give way when a person shows by his own act that he is relying on a different mode. Compare one who meant to lift a cup and raised it too little, but in doing so pulled it toward him: does the pulling acquire, when he meant to lift?

Tosafot: the one who takes the grain from under him is not even called a *rasha* (wicked). Snatching what another is about to obtain is wicked only where the snatcher could find the same elsewhere; a find or *pe'ah* is a one-time chance.

children.title: Rav Pappa: *Arba Amot* Don't Acquire in a Landowner's Field
children.gist: Rav Pappa answers differently: the Sages enacted *arba amot* for public land, not for a field that has an owner. The Torah let the poor man walk in the field and collect *pe'ah*, but did not make the field his courtyard.

bullets.text: Rav Pappa: the enactment of *arba amot* applies in the world at large, on public land, but not in a field that belongs to an owner.

The poor man does have rights in the owner's field during the gathering of *pe'ah*. But the Torah gave him the right to walk there and collect, not the right that the field count as his courtyard for acquiring.
Since the *arba amot* work as a personal courtyard, they can't override the landowner's real hold on the ground the poor man stands on.

children.title: The Objection from Our Mishnah: The Finder Who Fell on His Find
children.gist: R. Ya'akov bar Idi asks the same about our Mishnah's finder: why don't his *arba amot* acquire the item before the other seizes it? The Gemara repeats its answer, and Rav Sheshet gives his own: the enactment doesn't apply in the crowded public domain.

bullets.text: R. Ya'akov bar Idi: our Mishnah gives the item to the one who seized it. If a person's *arba amot* acquire for him everywhere, the one who fell, with the item inside his 4 cubits, should already own it.

children.title: Our Finder Also Showed He Chose Falling over His *Arba Amot*
children.gist: The Gemara gives the same answer as before. A declaration is not needed, but the finder who fell showed he wanted to acquire by falling and not through the enactment, so he acquired nothing.

bullets.text: First the Gemara says he didn't declare “I will acquire it”, then asks why a declaration should matter for an enactment.
It answers that by falling he showed he wants to acquire by falling, not through his *arba amot*; having given up the Sages' mode, he doesn't acquire the item.

returns_to.note: The same answer the Gemara gave to the objection from *pe'ah*

children.title: Rav Sheshet: *Arba Amot* Acquire in an Alleyway, Not Where Crowds Press
children.gist: Rav Sheshet answers that the Sages enacted *arba amot* for a *simta* (a side alley), not for the *reshut ha'rabim* (public domain), where crowds press. Reish Lakish's “everywhere” comes to include the sides of the public domain.

bullets.text: Rav Sheshet: the enactment applies in a place like an alleyway, where the crowds don't press, so the 4 cubits around a person can count as his for the moment.
In the public domain, where crowds press, the Sages did not enact it. So our Mishnah's finder, if he stood in the public domain, had no *arba amot* to acquire for him.
The Gemara asks: didn't Reish Lakish say “everywhere”? Answer: “everywhere” includes the sides of the public domain, next to it but not part of it, where the crowds don't press.

In a pressing crowd there is no personal space to speak of, so the idea the enactment rests on falls away. The shiur compares the rule that pulling an item acquires in a *simta* but not in the public domain.

sections.title: Can a *Ketanah* Acquire Through Her *Chatzer* or Her *Arba Amot*?
sections.gist: Reish Lakish, in the name of Abba Kohen Bardela, says a *ketanah* (minor girl) acquires through neither her *chatzer* (one's property acquiring for its owner) nor her *arba amot*; R. Yochanan, in the name of R. Yannai, says she acquires through both. The Gemara traces this to whether a *chatzer* acquires as one's hand or as one's agent, and then asks how a *chatzer* could be an agent when it can commit theft for its owner.
sections.continues: Continues at 10b.15: the practical difference between Ravina's and Rav Samma's answers, and then the question whether anyone denies that a *chatzer* works as one's hand, from the baraita on a *get* placed in a woman's courtyard.

children.title: R. Yannai vs. Abba Kohen Bardela: Does a *Chatzer* Acquire as a Hand or as an Agent?
children.gist: R. Yannai holds that a *chatzer* is included as one's hand, and a minor girl has a hand, so she acquires through it. Abba Kohen Bardela holds it is included as *shelichut*, and a minor can't appoint an agent, so she has no *chatzer*.

bullets.text: Reish Lakish in the name of Abba Kohen Bardela: a *ketanah* has no *chatzer* and no *arba amot* to acquire for her. R. Yochanan in the name of R. Yannai: she has both.
R. Yannai: a *chatzer* was included as a means of acquiring because it is like her hand. Just as a minor girl acquires with her hand, she acquires through her courtyard.
Abba Kohen Bardela: a *chatzer* was included because of *shelichut*. A minor has no power of agency, since she can't appoint an agent, so her courtyard can't acquire for her either.

On the first view the courtyard is the owner's own reach extended; on the second it takes possession on her behalf, almost as a representative. The *arba amot*, a portable courtyard, follow whichever view one takes of the *chatzer*.

chart.title: R. Yannai vs. Abba Kohen Bardela: can a minor girl acquire through her courtyard and her 4 cubits?
rows: Abba Kohen Bardela, reported by Reish Lakish
**They do not acquire for her**
*Shelichut*: a minor can't appoint an agent, so her courtyard can't act for her
R. Yannai, reported by R. Yochanan
**They acquire for her**
Her hand: a minor acquires with her hand, so also with her courtyard

children.title: Why Can a *Chatzer* Commit Theft for Its Owner, When an Agent Can't?
children.gist: A baraita makes a thief liable for double payment when the stolen animal is found in his yard, as if in his hand. If a *chatzer* were an agent, *ein shaliach li'dvar aveirah* (there is no agency for a transgression) should keep the theft from counting as his. Ravina answers that the rule applies only to an agent who is *bar chiyuva* (himself subject to the prohibition); Rav Samma, only to an agent who could choose to refuse.

bullets.text: Baraita on “If the theft is found in his hand” (Shemot 22:3): “in his hand” teaches only his hand. The doubled phrase *himatze timatze* adds his roof, his yard and his enclosure, so a theft found anywhere in his domain makes him liable.

The Gemara asks: if a *chatzer* acquires as an agent, this would be agency for a transgression. Yet one who sends an agent to transgress is not liable; the agent is, and his act isn't counted as the sender's.
With a human agent, no theft is credited to the sender at all, so he bears no liability for it. If the *chatzer* were such an agent, the stolen animal in the yard should be no theft of the owner's.

chart.title: Ravina vs. Rav Samma: why a *chatzer* makes its owner liable for theft

When the agent is himself *bar chiyuva*, subject to the prohibition
A courtyard is not subject to the prohibition, so the liability stays with its owner
Rav Samma
When the agent can choose to carry out the errand or refuse it
Items are placed in a courtyard without its consent, so the liability stays with its owner

children.title: Ravina: Only an Agent Bound by the Prohibition Takes the Liability
children.gist: Ravina holds that liability passes to the agent only where he is himself subject to the prohibition; a *chatzer* is not, so its owner is liable. A woman or slave sent to steal is no exception: they are bound by the prohibition and will pay once divorced or freed.

bullets.text: Ravina: “there is no agency for a transgression” applies where the agent is *bar chiyuva*, so he, not the sender, is liable. A *chatzer* is not subject to liability, so its sender, the owner, is liable.

The rule rests on the agent's duty to obey God rather than the one who sent him: having chosen to transgress, he bears it. A courtyard is commanded by no one, so nothing stands between the owner and the theft.
The Gemara objects: then one who tells a married woman or a slave “go steal for me” should be liable, since they have no property to pay from.

Answer: a woman and a slave are subject to the prohibition; they simply can't pay now. The Mishnah (Bava Kamma 87a) rules that if the woman is divorced or the slave freed, they must pay for damage they did, so the liability is theirs.

children.title: Rav Samma: Only an Agent Free to Refuse Takes the Liability
children.gist: Rav Samma holds that liability passes to the agent only where he could carry out the errand or refuse it. Items are placed in a *chatzer* without its consent, so its owner is liable.

bullets.text: Rav Samma: “there is no agency for a transgression” applies where the agent could do the errand if he wished and refrain if he wished. A courtyard has things placed in it without its consent, so its owner is liable.
With no free choice in between, the courtyard is only an instrument of its owner. Here, then, agency does carry over a transgression, because the “agent” can't take the responsibility on itself.

key_terms.sense: lifting a found item on behalf of another
key_terms.definition: One who performs the act of lifting an ownerless found item in order that another person acquire it. The question is whether the other person acquires it through that lifting.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda rule that the other does not acquire, while R. Yochanan rules that he does; each reads the rider Mishnah accordingly.

key_terms.term: tofes le'ba'al chov bi'mkom she'chav la'acherim
key_terms.hebrew: תופס לבעל חוב במקום שחב לאחרים
key_terms.sense: seizing for one creditor to the detriment of others
key_terms.definition: A third party who seizes a debtor's assets on behalf of one creditor where the debtor owes other creditors as well. Such a seizure does not acquire for the creditor, since it favors him at the others' expense.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda compare lifting a found item for another to such a seizure, since everyone has an equal right to the item.
aliases: tofes le'ba'al chov bi'mkom she'chav la'acherim

key_terms.sense: a hired laborer's hand as his employer's
key_terms.definition: The principle that while a laborer works for his employer, his acts of acquisition within the scope of his hire count as the employer's own.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Nachman uses it to explain why a laborer hired for “any work” finds for his employer, and holds that the laborer's right to quit doesn't undo it.

key_terms.sense: the corner of the field left for the poor
key_terms.definition: The portion of a field's crop that the owner must leave unharvested for the poor, who come into the field and gather it.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Mishnah in Pe'ah, where a poor man who falls on the *pe'ah* acquires nothing, is the first objection to Reish Lakish's *arba amot*.

key_terms.sense: acquisition through the 4 cubits around a person
key_terms.definition: A rabbinic enactment by which the area of 4 cubits around a person acquires ownerless items for him, as if it were his courtyard.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Reish Lakish states it in the name of Abba Kohen Bardela; the Gemara explains why it doesn't help one who fell on a find, Rav Pappa excludes a landowner's field and Rav Sheshet the public domain, and the Amoraim dispute whether a minor girl has it.

key_terms.definition: A person's courtyard or other property acquires for him objects that enter it, as a means of *kinyan*, sometimes even without his knowledge.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Gemara asks whether a *chatzer* acquires as one's hand or as one's agent, and how it can make its owner liable for theft if it is an agent.

key_terms.definition: The appointment of an agent whose acts count as those of the one who sent him. Appointing an agent requires legal capacity, which a minor lacks.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Abba Kohen Bardela bases *chatzer* on *shelichut*, so a minor girl, who can't appoint an agent, has no *chatzer*.

key_terms.definition: The principle that an agent sent to commit a transgression bears the responsibility himself, and his act is not attributed to the one who sent him.
key_terms.on_this_daf: A stolen item found in a thief's yard makes him liable, so the Gemara asks why this principle doesn't apply if a *chatzer* is an agent; Ravina and Rav Samma limit its scope.

key_terms.sense: one subject to a legal obligation
key_terms.definition: A person bound by the commandment or liability in question, as opposed to one to whom it does not apply.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Ravina holds that liability passes to an agent only if he is *bar chiyuva*; a courtyard is not, while a woman or slave is, even when they can't pay.

quiz.q: A rider tells a pedestrian “Give me that found item.” The pedestrian lifts it, hands it to the rider, and only then says “I acquired it for myself at the outset.” What is the rule?
options: He has said nothing, and the rider keeps the item
The pedestrian takes it back, since he lifted it for himself
They divide the item, each with an oath
The item is set aside until the truth is known
quiz.why: Once the item is in the rider's hands, the pedestrian's claim is worthless; the Gemara only debates what the clause's “at the outset” implies for the first clause.

quiz.q: Why do Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda rule that one who lifts a found item for a friend does not acquire it for the friend?
options: It is like seizing a debtor's goods for one creditor at the other creditors' expense
A found item can be acquired only by pulling, not by lifting
The friend never told him to acquire it
One cannot acquire anything without being its owner
quiz.why: Everyone has an equal right to a find, and taking that chance from all the others for one person is *tofes le'ba'al chov bi'mkom she'chav la'acherim*.

quiz.q: An employer hires a laborer saying “work for me today,” and the laborer finds a lost item. Who keeps it, and why?
options: The employer, since finding counts as work and the laborer's hand is like his employer's
The laborer, since he wasn't hired to look for finds
The laborer, since a laborer may quit even at midday
They divide it, since both had a part in it
quiz.why: With no task specified, finding falls within the hire, and by *yad po'el ke'yad ba'al ha'bayit* the employer acquires through him; had he said “weed for me today,” the laborer would keep it.

quiz.q: Why may a hired laborer quit his job even at midday?
options: “They are My slaves, not slaves of slaves”: a Jew may not be bound to another
Because his hand is not truly his employer's hand
Because the employer gains nothing from half a day's work
Because a hire for a day is never binding
quiz.why: Rav Nachman grounds the right to quit in Vayikra 25:55; until the laborer quits, his hand is still his employer's.

quiz.q: According to R. Yochanan, lifting a found item for another acquires it for him. Why, then, may the Mishnah's pedestrian keep the item the rider asked for?
options: The rider said “give it to me,” not “acquire it for me,” so he acquires only when he receives it
The pedestrian claimed he meant it for himself from the start
Lifting can never acquire for someone riding an animal
The rider had already passed the item
quiz.why: Asked only to deliver it, the pedestrian lifted it without acquiring for the rider; “acquire it for me” would have made it the rider's at once.

quiz.q: A poor man falls on *pe'ah* that lies within the 4 cubits around him. Why don't his *arba amot* acquire it, according to the Gemara's first answer?
options: By falling he showed he wanted to acquire by falling, not by his *arba amot*
He didn't declare that he wished to acquire it
*Arba amot* never acquire produce
The *pe'ah* belongs to all the poor together
quiz.why: A declaration isn't needed for the enactment, but choosing to acquire by falling, which is no *kinyan*, gives up the Sages' mode.

quiz.q: According to Rav Sheshet, where do a person's *arba amot* fail to acquire for him?
options: In the public domain, where the crowds press
In an alleyway, where few people pass
At the sides of the public domain
In any field, whoever owns it
quiz.why: In a crowd the 4 cubits around a person can't count as his; “everywhere” extends only to the sides of the public domain.

quiz.q: A stolen animal is found in a man's yard, and a baraita holds him liable. According to Ravina, why doesn't “there is no agency for a transgression” protect him, if a *chatzer* is an agent?
options: The rule applies only to an agent who is himself subject to the prohibition, and a courtyard is not
The rule applies only to an agent who could refuse, and a courtyard can't
A courtyard acquires as his hand, not as an agent
The owner locked the gate himself
quiz.why: Ravina limits the rule to an agent who is *bar chiyuva*; Rav Samma limits it instead to an agent free to refuse.

judgment_calls: The opening exchange (10a.3–4) is its own top-level section rather than a child of the question whether lifting for another acquires (s2): it is the tail of Ulla and Rav Nachman's debate from 9b about reading the Mishnah, while s2 opens with Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda's explicit ruling. R. Yochanan's reading is linked back to it with returns_to.

The laborer passage (10a.7–11) is nested under s2 with two children, since both Rava's objection and the right to quit serve only to test Rav Nachman's ruling; the verse about slaves could have been a section of its own but is part of Rav Nachman's defense.

The Mishnah of falling on a find (10a.13) is a separate top-level section from Reish Lakish's *arba amot*, though the Gemara uses it as the second objection; the Mishnah's own ruling is self-contained, and the objection from it is outlined where it falls (s14).

Each objection to *arba amot* is a parent with its answers as children, so Rav Pappa sits under the *pe'ah* objection and Rav Sheshet under the objection from our Mishnah, following where the text places them. Both could instead be read as general limits on the enactment.
The theft discussion (10b.9–14) is nested under the minor girl dispute rather than made top-level, since it is the Gemara's challenge to Abba Kohen Bardela's view that a *chatzer* works as agency.
coverage_notes: The shiur's material on 9b and 10a.1–2 (the start of Ulla and Rav Nachman's debate) falls before this outline's scope; only 10a.3 onward is outlined. Its material on 10b.15 onward (the practical difference between the answers, and the *get* baraita) falls after it.
The essay calls the second answer on agency for a transgression “Rava's better answer”; the text attributes it to Rav Samma (10b.14). Followed the text.

The essay at one point assigns the view that a *chatzer* is like one's hand to Reish Lakish before correcting itself; the text has R. Yannai (cited by R. Yochanan) hold that a *chatzer* is her hand, and Abba Kohen Bardela (cited by Reish Lakish) that it is agency. Followed the text.

The essay frames the minor girl dispute as being about receiving a *get*; within these lines the text states it generally, and at 10b.17–18 (outside scope) the Gemara says all agree on a *get* and the dispute is about a found item. The outline describes it generally and does not call it a dispute about a *get*.

The essay presents the second objection to *arba amot* only as part of a general heading; the text has R. Ya'akov bar Idi object from our Mishnah (10b.2) and the Gemara repeat its answer (10b.3), outlined separately.
The essay describes the Gemara's first answer to the *pe'ah* objection as rejected; the text questions it and then refines it into the answer that falling reveals his intent. Followed the text.
The essay's account of Tosafot on *rasha* (a land case in Kiddushin) is unclear; it is given generally as a shiur bullet.

The essay's remarks on Rabbeinu Tam and drawing water from a public well, on *eiruvin* and *techumin*, and on *arba amot* for a *get* being rabbinic yet effective by Torah law, are left out as tangential.

daf_summary.summary: Discussion of: how to read the rider Mishnah (Ulla: the pedestrian claimed it at the outset; Rav Nachman: he keeps it regardless); whether lifting a find for another acquires (Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda: no, like seizing for one creditor; R. Yochanan: yes), with the laborer who finds for his employer and may quit midday; the Mishnah of one who falls on a find; Reish Lakish's *arba amot* and its limits (falling shows other intent, Rav Pappa's owner's field, Rav Sheshet's public domain); and whether a minor girl acquires through her *chatzer* and *arba amot*, which leads to why a *chatzer* can commit theft for its owner (Ravina vs. Rav Samma).

takeaways.text: Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda hold that lifting a found item for another doesn't acquire it for him, since it takes away a chance that belongs equally to everyone, like seizing a debtor's goods for one creditor; R. Yochanan holds it does, unless the other asked only to be handed the item.
A laborer hired for “any work” finds for his employer, because his hand is like his employer's; he may still quit at midday, since a Jew may not be bound to another as a slave.

The Sages enacted that the 4 cubits around a person acquire for him, so that people won't quarrel; but one who falls on an item shows he relies on falling, which is no *kinyan*, and the enactment doesn't apply in a landowner's field (Rav Pappa) or the crowded public domain (Rav Sheshet).
Whether a minor girl acquires through her courtyard depends on whether a *chatzer* is her hand (R. Yannai) or her agent (Abba Kohen Bardela), since a minor can't appoint an agent.

A stolen item found in a thief's yard makes him liable even if a *chatzer* is an agent, since the rule that there is no agency for a transgression applies only to an agent bound by the prohibition (Ravina) or free to refuse (Rav Samma).

debates.question: Does lifting a found item on behalf of another acquire it for him?

sides.view: No: it is like seizing for one creditor at the others' expense

sides.who: R. Yochanan, reported by R. Chiyya bar Abba
sides.view: Yes: the Mishnah's rider asked only to be handed the item

debates.question: Why don't the *arba amot* of one who fell on a find acquire it for him?

sides.view: Falling showed he chose to acquire by falling
The enactment doesn't apply in a landowner's field
The enactment doesn't apply in the crowded public domain

debates.outcome: Each answer stands; Reish Lakish's “everywhere” is read to include the sides of the public domain.

debates.question: Does a *chatzer* acquire as one's hand or as one's agent?

sides.view: As her hand, so a minor girl acquires through it
As agency, so a minor girl, who can't appoint an agent, does not

debates.outcome: The agency view survives the theft objection, which Ravina and Rav Samma answer in different ways.

debates.question: When does the rule that there is no agency for a transgression apply?

sides.view: When the agent is himself subject to the prohibition
When the agent can choose to refuse
